docs.title: Ethical Hacking
docs.text: Hands-on · CEH-aligned

docs.title: Attack it. Defend it. Report it.
docs.text:
A hands-on, CEH-aligned introduction to ethical hacking — you'll scan, test, exploit, and secure systems in a safe virtual lab, then learn to write up what you found like a professional.

4.5 units 48 lecture + 18 lab hrs CEH exam-aligned Hands-on ACI Skill Labs Open-access readings — $0

docs.title: Weekly schedule
docs.text: The course follows the real attacker's kill chain across five phases, covering the full set of CEH topic areas. Each week is a single notes page with its reading and a link to that week's hands-on ACI lab.

docs.title: Foundation
docs.text:
The rules before the tools — ethics, authorization, and the five-phase methodology that frames everything.

Week Topic Week 1 Ethics, Law & Methodology

docs.title: Recon & Scanning
docs.text:
Profile the target, then find what's reachable — footprinting, OSINT, network scanning with Nmap, and enumeration.

Week Topic Week 2 Reconnaissance & Footprinting Week 3 Scanning & Enumeration

docs.title: Network & Crypto
docs.text:
Listen on the wire and slip past defenses — then the cryptography that protects data and how it fails.

Week Topic Week 4 Network Hacking & Sniffing Week 5 Cryptography — PKI, certificates, attacks

docs.title: System & Malware
docs.text:
Break into Windows and Linux hosts, then understand the malware, DoS, and session hijacking that follow.

Week Topic Week 6 System Attacks — Windows/Linux · Midterm Week 7 Trojans, Malware & DoS

docs.title: Human & Web
docs.text:
Exploit people and the web — social engineering, web-server and web-app attacks, and a SQL-injection deep dive.

Week Topic Week 8 Social Engineering · Ethics paper Week 9 Web Attacks I — servers & apps Week 10 Web Attacks II — SQL Injection

docs.title: Wireless & Pentest
docs.text:
Attacks that travel through the air, then a full penetration test and a professional findings report.

Week Topic Week 11 Wireless Hacking (WEP/WPA) Week 12 Penetration Testing · Capstone + Final

docs.title: What you'll be able to do
docs.text:
By the end of the quarter you will be able to demonstrate the ability to attack and defend a network — the course's core learning outcome — and you'll be prepared for the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) exam. Concretely, you'll be able to:

  • Conduct reconnaissance and map a target's attack surface.
  • Scan and enumerate hosts, services, and vulnerabilities.
  • Exploit systems and web applications in a controlled lab.
  • Recognize and reason about malware, DoS, and social-engineering attacks.
  • Apply cryptographic concepts and evade basic network defenses.
  • Plan a penetration test and write a professional findings report.

docs.title: How the course is delivered
docs.text:
Three moving parts

Lecture (concepts, in class) · Labs (hands-on, ACI Skill Labs) · Reading (free, open-access — linked on every week page). There is no textbook to buy.

  • Hands-on labs run on ACI Skill Labs. Every lab includes a guided walkthrough, a live virtual machine, and auto-graded checkpoints.
  • Readings are all free and open-access — NIST guides, OWASP, the official Nmap book, Crypto 101, Metasploit Unleashed, and more. See the Free Resource Library.
  • Ethics and law run through the whole course, anchored by Alana Maurushat's open-access Ethical Hacking.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Read the Syllabus for policies, grading, and the week-1 setup steps.
  • New to the tools? Skim Kali Linux Revealed before Week 3.
  • Jump to Week 1.

Authorization first

Everything in this course is practiced only inside the provided lab environment or on systems you have explicit written permission to test. Unauthorized access to computer systems is a crime. You'll sign an acceptable-use agreement in Week 1.

docs.title: Course description
docs.text:
Students will scan, test, hack, and secure systems; implement perimeter defenses; and scan and attack virtual networks. Coverage includes intrusion detection, social engineering, footprinting, DDoS attacks, buffer overflows, SQL injection, privilege escalation, trojans, backdoors, and wireless hacking, with emphasis on legal and ethical guidelines. The course prepares students for the Certified Ethical Hacker (C|EH) exam.

Format Lecture + hands-on lab Course outcome Demonstrate the ability to attack and defend a network. Advisories Prior coursework in networking and operating systems recommended Textbook None to buy — all readings are free/open-access Lab platform ACI Skill Labs

docs.title: Course objectives
docs.text:
1. Explore ethical hacking fundamentals
  2. Explore cryptographic concepts
  3. Investigate reconnaissance and information gathering
  4. Explore scanning and enumeration
  5. Explore network hacking via sniffers and evasion
  6. Investigate system attacks
  7. Explore low-tech hacking techniques
  8. Investigate web-based hacking
  9. Explore wireless network hacking
  10. Investigate trojans and related attacks
  11. Perform penetration testing

docs.text: Component Weight Notes Hands-on labs (auto-graded) 35% ACI Skill Labs — Performance Reports Midterm exam 15% Units 1–6, CEH-style Final exam 15% Cumulative, CEH-style Capstone penetration-test report 20% Methodology + professional deliverable Ethics paper + participation 15% Maurushat-based paper, discussions

docs.title: Week-1 setup checklist
docs.text:
Do these in the first week

  1. Get your institutional email set up (needed for any external sign-ups).
  2. Log in to the ACI Skill Labs portal and confirm you can launch a lab VM (the Start button) — run the Week-2 recon lab's intro to test it.
  3. Bookmark the Free Resource Library.
  4. Read and sign the Acceptable-Use / Authorization Agreement.
  5. Skim Maurushat, Ethical Hacking, Introduction (open-access — see Week 1).

docs.title: Academic integrity & ethics
docs.text: The skills in this course are powerful and, misused, illegal. You will practice them only in the provided lab environment or against systems you have explicit written authorization to test. Any attack against systems, networks, or accounts without authorization is a violation of course policy and of state and federal law, and may result in course failure and possible referral. When in doubt, ask before you act.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text: Students who need accommodations should contact their institution's disability support office and let the instructor know early in the term so arrangements can be made for lecture, labs, and exams.

docs.title: Week 1 · Ethics, Law & Methodology
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 1 · Ethics, Law & Methodology
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • What ethical hacking is — and the legal line that defines it
  • Authorization, scope, and rules of engagement
  • The five-phase methodology that structures the whole course
  • Getting your lab access set up

Lab this week: Introduction to AI in Ethical Hacking (setup) · Reading: Maurushat + NIST SP 800-115

docs.title: 1. What is ethical hacking?
docs.text: An ethical hacker uses the same tools and techniques as an attacker, but with permission and for defense. White, grey, and black hats differ not in skill but in authorization and intent. The whole point: think like an attacker so you can defend like a professional.

docs.title: 2. Types of assessment
docs.text:
• Vulnerability assessment — find and list weaknesses.
  • Penetration test — actively exploit them to show real impact.
  • Red team — simulate a full adversary against people, process, and technology.

docs.title: 3. The legal & professional frame
docs.text: What separates a penetration test from a crime is written authorization. Before any testing: a signed scope, rules of engagement, and (often) a non-disclosure agreement. Unauthorized access is a crime under laws like the U.S. CFAA and state statutes. When in doubt, stop and confirm scope.

docs.title: 4. The five-phase methodology
docs.text:
1. Reconnaissance — gather information
  2. Scanning — find live hosts, ports, services
  3. Gaining access — exploit
  4. Maintaining access — persistence
  5. Covering tracks — anti-forensics

Every later week maps onto one of these phases.

docs.title: 5. Where the line blurs
docs.text: Hacktivism operates in a legal and ethical grey zone. We'll use the Maurushat reading to discuss where "ethical" hacking ends and civil disobedience or crime begins.

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — setup

Launch Introduction to AI in Ethical Hacking to confirm your access works end to end: check that the Start button spins up a VM and that Performance Reports records your completion. No attack lab this week.

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:

  • Sign the Acceptable-Use / Authorization Agreement.

docs.title: Week 2 · Reconnaissance & Footprinting
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 2 · Reconnaissance & Footprinting
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Passive vs. active reconnaissance
  • WHOIS, DNS, and subdomain discovery
  • OSINT techniques and search operators
  • How a footprint feeds everything that follows

Lab this week: Recon labs · Reading: NIST SP 800-115 §4, OSINT Framework

docs.title: 1. Passive vs. active recon
docs.text: Passive recon uses public information and never touches the target directly — it's stealthy and low-risk. Active recon interacts with the target (and starts to carry legal weight). You always start passive.

docs.title: 2. WHOIS & DNS
docs.text: Registrars, name servers, and DNS records reveal domains, IP ranges, mail servers, and often subdomains. Certificate-transparency logs are a goldmine for discovering hosts an organization didn't mean to expose.

docs.title: 3. OSINT
docs.text: Open-source intelligence — search-engine operators ("dorking"), job postings, employee social media, document metadata, and breach data — builds a picture of people, technologies, and exposure before you send a single scan.

docs.title: 4. The footprint
docs.text: The output of this week is a target profile: domains, hosts, emails, technologies, and exposed services. That profile drives your scanning (Week 3) and your social-engineering pretexts (Week 8).

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Footprinting and Reconnaissance Techniques with AI (primer) and Performing Reconnaissance from the WAN (graded). Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.text:

  • OSINT Framework. osintframework.com
  • MITRE ATT&CK — Reconnaissance (TA0043). attack.mitre.org

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: Footprint a provided practice domain and submit a one-page recon summary: assets found, methods used, and what a defender should hide.

docs.title: Week 3 · Scanning & Enumeration
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 3 · Scanning & Enumeration
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • The main scan types and when to use each
  • Nmap for host discovery, service/OS detection, and scripting
  • Turning open ports into real intel through enumeration
  • How scanning looks from the defender's side

Lab this week: Scanning + Enumeration labs · Reading: Nmap book, NIST SP 800-115

docs.title: 1. Why scan?
docs.text:
Reconnaissance told you who the target is. Scanning tells you what's reachable — which hosts are up, which ports are open, and what's listening. It's the bridge between "here's a domain" and "here's an exploitable service."

Passive recon (Week 2) Active scanning (this week) 🕵️ No packets to the target 📡 You send probes to the target Public data, OSINT, WHOIS/DNS Live host & port discovery Stealthy, low legal risk Noisy — authorization required

docs.title: 2. Scan types
docs.text:
• TCP connect scan — completes the full handshake. Reliable, but loud and logged.
  • SYN ("half-open") scan — sends SYN, never finishes. Faster and quieter.
  • UDP scan — for DNS, SNMP, DHCP. Slower and trickier to read.

Every port comes back as open, closed, or filtered (a firewall is dropping the probe).

docs.title: 3. Nmap in depth
docs.text:
Host discovery — who's alive? 
nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24      # ping sweep, no port scan
Service & version detection 
nmap -sV -p- 10.0.0.5     # all ports, identify service versions
OS fingerprint + default scripts 
nmap -O -sC 10.0.0.5      # OS guess + safe NSE scripts

docs.title: 4. Enumeration
docs.text:
Scanning finds the door; enumeration reads the nameplate. Pull detail out of a discovered service:

  • SMB — shares, users, domains
  • SNMP — device config (watch for the public community string)
  • SMTP — valid usernames via VRFY/RCPT

The goal: convert "a port is open" into "here's the version, the users, and the shares."

docs.title: 5. The defender's view
docs.text: A ping sweep and a full port scan light up IDS signatures and firewall logs. Knowing what scanning looks like to a defender is exactly what makes you good at the "defend" half of the course — and it previews next week's IDS/firewall material.

docs.title: Week 4 · Network Hacking & Sniffing
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 4 · Network Hacking & Sniffing
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Capturing and reading network traffic
  • ARP spoofing / man-in-the-middle
  • IDS, firewalls, and honeypots — and evasion

Lab this week: Sniffer + firewall-evasion labs · Reading: Wireshark guide, MITRE ATT&CK

docs.title: 1. Sniffing
docs.text: A sniffer captures packets off the wire. On a switched network you need active techniques — ARP poisoning to become a man-in-the-middle — to see traffic that isn't yours. Cleartext protocols leak credentials directly.

docs.title: 2. Reading traffic
docs.text: With Wireshark you follow TCP streams, filter by protocol, and extract data. This is where "the network is the attack surface" becomes concrete — and why encryption matters.

docs.title: 3. Network defenses
docs.text:
• IDS/IPS — signature and anomaly detection.
  • Firewalls — stateful and application-layer rule sets.
  • Honeypots — decoys that catch and study attackers.

docs.title: 4. Evasion
docs.text: Attackers tunnel, encrypt, and fragment to slip past defenses. Exfiltrating data over an encrypted channel is hard to detect — which is exactly what this week's second lab demonstrates.

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Capturing and Analyzing Network Traffic Using a Sniffer and Attacking the Firewall and Stealing Data Over an Encrypted Channel. Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.title: Reading (free)
docs.text:

  • MITRE ATT&CK — Network Sniffing (T1040) · Defense Evasion (TA0005). T1040 · TA0005

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: From a provided capture, identify the protocol, extract the leaked data, and recommend one defense.

docs.title: Week 5 · Cryptography
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 5 · Cryptography
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption
  • PKI: keys, certificates, and certificate authorities
  • Hashing, signatures, and common crypto attacks

Lab this week: Cryptography + Public Key labs · Reading: Crypto 101

docs.title: 1. Symmetric vs. asymmetric
docs.text: Symmetric (AES) uses one shared key — fast, but key distribution is the hard part. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses a public/private pair, which solves key exchange and enables signatures.

docs.title: 2. PKI
docs.text: Public Key Infrastructure ties a public key to an identity through certificates signed by a certificate authority. This is the trust model behind HTTPS: chains of trust, X.509 certificates, and the TLS handshake.

docs.title: 3. Hashing & integrity
docs.text: Hashes (SHA-2) verify integrity and store passwords — but a hash is not encryption. Salting defends against precomputed (rainbow-table) attacks.

docs.title: 4. Attacks
docs.text: Brute force, birthday attacks, downgrade attacks, and weak-key/weak-configuration issues. Most real-world crypto failures are implementation and configuration mistakes, not broken math.

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Cryptography Techniques with AI (primer) and Using Public Key Encryption to Secure Messages (graded). Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.title: Reading (free)
docs.text: • Crypto 101 (free book) — Ch. 1–7 (block/stream ciphers, key exchange, public-key, hashes). crypto101.io

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: Generate a keypair, sign and verify a message, and explain in a paragraph what a certificate adds on top of a raw public key.

docs.title: Week 6 · System Attacks (Midterm)
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 6 · System Attacks · Midterm
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Exploiting Windows and Linux systems
  • Privilege escalation and post-exploitation
  • Using Metasploit to deliver and manage an exploit

Lab this week: Exploitation labs · Reading: Metasploit Unleashed, Kali Revealed · Midterm this week

docs.title: 1. Exploitation basics
docs.text: Match a vulnerability to an exploit, deliver a payload, and get a shell. Payloads range from a simple reverse shell to a full Meterpreter session.

docs.title: 2. Metasploit
docs.text: The framework that standardizes this: modules, msfconsole, and Meterpreter for post-exploitation. It's how one operator manages exploits, payloads, and sessions consistently.

docs.title: 3. Privilege escalation
docs.text: Landing on a box is rarely the end — you usually arrive as a low-privileged user. Windows and Linux each have well-known escalation paths (misconfigurations, weak permissions, credential reuse).

docs.title: 4. Post-exploitation
docs.text: Persistence, pivoting to other hosts, and covering tracks — and, crucially, the artifacts each of these leaves behind for defenders to catch.

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Remote and Local Exploitation and Using Browser Exploitation to Take Over a Host's Computer. Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.text:
• Metasploit Unleashed (OffSec, free). offsec.com/metasploit-unleashed
  • Kali Linux Revealed (official, free). kali.org book

docs.text: Complete both labs. Midterm exam covers Units 1–6 (CEH-style).

docs.title: Week 7 · Trojans, Malware & DoS
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 7 · Trojans, Malware & DoS
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Malware types: viruses, worms, trojans, RATs
  • How a RAT is built, delivered, and detected
  • Denial-of-service and session hijacking

Lab this week: RAT + DoS labs · Reading: MITRE ATT&CK, CISA

docs.title: 1. Malware taxonomy
docs.text: Distinguish propagation (how it spreads: virus, worm) from payload (what it does: backdoor, ransomware, RAT). A Remote Access Trojan gives an attacker ongoing control of a compromised host.

docs.title: 2. RAT lifecycle
docs.text: Build → deliver → command-and-control → persist. Understanding each stage tells a defender exactly where to place detection and prevention.

docs.title: 3. Denial of service
docs.text: Volumetric, protocol, and application-layer attacks — and amplification, where a small request triggers a huge response. DDoS spreads the source across many hosts.

docs.title: 4. Session hijacking
docs.text: Stealing or forging a session token lets an attacker ride a legitimate user's authenticated session. It's why HTTPS and secure, HttpOnly cookies matter.

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Crafting and Deploying Malware Using a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) and Performing a Denial of Service Attack from the WAN. Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.title: Reading (free)
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — Command & Control (TA0011) · Endpoint DoS (T1499). TA0011 · T1499
  • CISA — Understanding Denial-of-Service Attacks. cisa.gov

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: For the RAT you deployed, list three detection or prevention controls a defender could use at different layers.

docs.title: Week 8 · Social Engineering
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 8 · Social Engineering
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • The psychology behind social-engineering attacks
  • Building a phishing scenario with SET
  • Awareness and technical defenses — and the ethics of pretexting

Lab this week: Social Engineering (SET) · Reading: MITRE ATT&CK, CISA, Maurushat · Ethics paper this week

docs.title: 1. Principles of influence
docs.text: Attackers exploit authority, urgency, reciprocity, and trust. The easiest exploit is often a person, not a system.

docs.title: 2. Vectors
docs.text: Phishing, spear-phishing, vishing (voice), pretexting, tailgating, and physical intrusion. Each targets a different human or physical control.

docs.title: 3. SET
docs.text: The Social-Engineer Toolkit builds credential-harvesting pages and payload-delivery scenarios — the hands-on lab this week.

docs.title: 4. Defense & ethics
docs.text: Awareness training, MFA, a healthy reporting culture, and technical filtering. And a hard question we'll debate from Maurushat: when is a social-engineering test itself ethical, given it depends on deception?

docs.title: Lab this week
docs.text:
ACI Skill Labs — hands-on & auto-graded

Complete Social Engineering Attacks Using SET. Launch from the ACI Skill Labs portal.

docs.title: Reading (free)
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — Phishing (T1566). attack.mitre.org
  • CISA — Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks. cisa.gov
  • Maurushat, Ethical Hacking — ethics of deception & consent.

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text: Ethics paper (~1000 words): When is a social-engineering test ethical? Argue a position using Maurushat and one real-world case.

docs.title: Week 9 · Web Attacks I
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 9 · Web Attacks I
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • The web-server and web-application attack surface
  • The OWASP Top 10 as a shared vocabulary
  • Exploiting a vulnerable web app

Lab this week: Webserver + web-app labs · Reading: OWASP Top 10 & WSTG

docs.title: 1. Web-server attacks
docs.text: Misconfiguration, default credentials, outdated components, and directory traversal. The server itself is a target before you ever reach the application.

docs.title: 2. Web-app attacks
docs.text: Broken access control, injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), cross-site request forgery (CSRF), and insecure design. The web is the single biggest attack surface most organizations expose.

docs.title: 3. The OWASP Top 10
docs.text: A community-maintained list of the most critical web risks — the vocabulary you'll use to classify and communicate findings for the rest of the course.

docs.title: 4. Methodology
docs.text: Map the app → discover inputs → exploit → document. This previews the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide you'll lean on in Week 10.

docs.title: Week 10 · Web Attacks II — SQLi
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 10 · Web Attacks II — SQL Injection
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • How SQL injection works and why it's still so damaging
  • In-band, blind, and error-based SQLi
  • Defenses: parameterized queries, validation, least privilege
  • XSS and CSRF as sibling attacks (lecture)

Lab this week: SQL injection labs · Reading: OWASP SQLi + cheat sheet

docs.title: 1. SQLi mechanics
docs.text: Untrusted input concatenated into a database query lets an attacker change the query's meaning — the classic ' OR 1=1 --. From there: dump data, bypass auth, sometimes reach the OS.

docs.title: 2. Variants
docs.text:
• Union-based — append your own result set.
  • Error-based — leak data through error messages.
  • Blind (boolean/time-based) — infer data when there's no visible output.

docs.title: 3. Automation
docs.text: Tools like sqlmap scale these techniques — useful to understand both as an attacker and to recognize the traffic as a defender.

docs.title: 4. Defense
docs.text: Prepared statements / parameterized queries are the real fix, backed by input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and a WAF. In lecture we'll relate XSS (stored/reflected) and CSRF as the other major injection-style web attacks.

docs.title: Week 11 · Wireless Hacking

docs.title: Week 11 · Wireless Hacking
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • Wi-Fi security: WEP, WPA/WPA2/WPA3
  • Capturing a handshake and cracking the key
  • Bluetooth attack surface (lecture)

Lab this week: WEP/WPA cracking · Reading: Aircrack-ng docs

docs.title: 1. Wireless architecture
docs.text: SSIDs, access points, association, and the WPA 4-way handshake. Attacks travel through the air, so range and monitor-mode capture matter.

docs.title: 2. WEP vs. WPA
docs.text: WEP is fundamentally broken (IV reuse) and crackable in minutes. WPA/WPA2 require capturing the handshake and running a dictionary/brute-force attack offline. WPA3 closes several of these gaps.

docs.title: 3. Aircrack-ng workflow
docs.text: Put the adapter in monitor mode → capture the handshake → crack against a wordlist. The lab walks the full sequence.

docs.title: 4. Bluetooth (lecture)
docs.text: Bluejacking, bluesnarfing, and BLE exposure — a smaller but real attack surface on modern devices.

docs.title: Week 12 · Penetration Testing & Capstone
docs.text:
What this page covers

  • A full penetration-testing methodology, end to end
  • Scoping an engagement and writing the report
  • Capstone + final exam

This week: capstone report + final exam · Reading: NIST SP 800-115, PTES

docs.title: 1. Methodology
docs.text: Pre-engagement → reconnaissance → scanning → exploitation → post-exploitation → reporting. Every week of this course was one link in that chain; now you run the whole thing.

docs.title: 2. Frameworks
docs.text: NIST SP 800-115, PTES, and OSSTMM each formalize the process. They matter because a repeatable methodology is what separates a professional test from random hacking.

docs.title: 3. Deliverables
docs.text: The report is the product: an executive summary, findings with severity (CVSS), evidence, and prioritized remediation. Clear communication to a non-technical stakeholder is a graded skill.

docs.title: 4. Professionalism
docs.text: Retesting, responsible disclosure, and client communication close the loop.
